title: The Second Life of Old Games
summary_es: Por qué algunos videojuegos siguen vivos años después gracias a los jugadores que los modifican.
prediction_prompt: Why do you think some people still play games that are ten or fifteen years old?

sentences.text: When a video game company stops updating a game, most players move on.
New games arrive every week, and old ones are quickly forgotten.
But some games refuse to die.
Years after their release, they are still played by thousands of people every day.
The reason is usually not the company that made them.
It is the players themselves.
These players are called modders.
A mod, short for modification, is a change that a player makes to a game.
Some mods are small: they fix a bug or make the text easier to read.
Others are huge, adding new maps, new characters or even a completely new story.
In a few famous cases, a mod became so popular that it turned into a successful game of its own.
Why do people spend hundreds of hours on work that nobody pays them for?
When researchers asked modders this question, most of them gave similar answers.
They wanted to learn new skills, they enjoyed solving problems, and they liked being part of a community.
Many also said that modding was a way to say thank you to a game they loved.
For some modders, it is also the start of a career.
Building a mod is a lot like building a real product.
You have to plan your work, write code, test it, listen to feedback and keep up with changes to the game.
Several game studios now look at mods when they choose new employees, because a good mod shows what a person can actually do.
Of course, modding is not always simple.
Some companies do not allow players to change their games, and modders sometimes break the rules without knowing it.
Mods can also contain viruses, so players need to download them from websites they trust.
Most modding communities have clear rules to protect their members.
Still, the relationship between companies and modders is getting better.
Some studios now release official tools that make modding easier, and a few even share the money from popular mods with the people who made them.
For many players, this is good news.
It means that the games they love will not disappear when the company moves on.
As one modder put it, a game is finished when people stop playing it, not when the company stops working on it.

language_focus.explanation_es: *Of course* concede un punto en contra («claro que…, es cierto que…»); *Still* vuelve a la idea principal a pesar de lo anterior («aun así»). Organizan los párrafos 5 y 6.
En *websites they trust* y *a game they loved* falta el pronombre relativo: *websites (that) they trust*. Se omite cuando es el objeto del verbo de la relativa.

glossary.def_en: to say or show that you will not do something
glossary.example: My old laptop refused to start this morning.

glossary.def_en: the time when something new is made available to the public
glossary.example: The game sold a million copies in the first week after its release.

glossary.def_en: a person who makes changes to a video game
glossary.def_es: persona que crea mods (modificaciones) de videojuegos
glossary.example: A group of modders translated the game into Spanish.

glossary.def_en: a change that a player makes to a video game
glossary.def_es: mod: modificación de un videojuego hecha por los jugadores
glossary.example: This mod adds new cars to the game.
glossary.note_es: También es verbo (*to mod a game*); *modding* es la actividad.

glossary.def_en: a change made to something to improve it or to make it different
glossary.example: With a small modification, the old engine worked again.

glossary.def_en: a mistake in a computer program
glossary.example: The update fixed a bug that closed the app.
The small project turned into a real company.

glossary.def_en: separate and independent; belonging only to itself
glossary.example: The band now has a studio of its own.

glossary.def_en: a group of people who share an interest or live in the same place
glossary.example: The game has a friendly online community.

glossary.def_en: comments that tell you how good or useful your work is
glossary.example: My teacher gave me useful feedback on my essay.

glossary.def_en: to learn about new changes and react to them
glossary.def_es: estar al día de, seguir el ritmo de
glossary.example: It's hard to keep up with all the new apps.

glossary.def_en: a person who works for a company

glossary.example: He looks quiet, but he's actually very funny.

glossary.def_en: to believe that someone or something is honest and safe
glossary.example: Only download apps from shops you trust.
It was raining. Still, we went for a walk.
glossary.note_es: Al principio de frase y con coma no significa «todavía».

glossary.def_en: (as someone put it) the way someone said it
glossary.example: As my teacher put it, practice beats talent.

tasks.prompt: What is the text mainly about?

options.text: Why companies stop updating their games
How players keep old games alive by changing them
How to become a professional game designer in a few years

tasks.rationale_es: El primer párrafo plantea el fenómeno (juegos que no mueren) y su causa: los propios jugadores. Los peligros y el empleo son partes secundarias.

tasks.prompt: Match paragraphs 3, 4 and 5 with the best heading. There is one extra heading.

headings.text: A new kind of game shop

tasks.rationale_es: P3 explica por qué trabajan gratis; P4, cómo puede llevar a un empleo; P5, los problemas y las normas. Nadie habla de una tienda.

tasks.prompt: According to paragraph 2, what can a small mod do?

options.text: Turn into a new game of its own
Correct a problem in the game

tasks.rationale_es: *fix a bug* = arreglar un error. Las historias y personajes nuevos son de los mods grandes (*Others are huge…*).

tasks.prompt: In paragraph 3, who does "them" refer to in "most of them gave similar answers"?
tasks.rationale_es: Los investigadores preguntan y los *modders* responden: *them* se refiere a los *modders*.

tasks.prompt: Which reason for modding is NOT mentioned in paragraph 3?
tasks.rationale_es: El párrafo empieza diciendo que nadie les paga. Las otras tres razones aparecen en p3s3 y p3s4.

tasks.prompt: In paragraph 4, "keep up with changes to the game" means…

options.text: write down every change in a notebook
try to stop the company from making changes
stay informed about the changes and adapt

tasks.rationale_es: *keep up with* = mantenerse al día y adaptarse. Si el juego cambia, el mod tiene que seguir funcionando.

tasks.prompt: All game companies let players change their games.
tasks.rationale_es: *Some companies do not allow players to change their games*: no todas lo permiten.
El texto dice que para algunos es el comienzo de una carrera, pero no dice a qué se dedica la mayoría.

tasks.prompt: What is the writer's attitude towards modding?

options.text: Afraid that it will harm the game industry

tasks.rationale_es: Reconoce problemas (*Of course, modding is not always simple*) pero vuelve a lo positivo (*Still…*, *this is good news*).

tasks.prompt: Why does the writer end with the modder's words?

options.text: To introduce a new topic for another article
To show that modders are angry
To sum up the main idea of the text

tasks.rationale_es: La cita resume la tesis: un juego vive mientras la gente lo juega, gracias a los jugadores.

tasks.prompt: Complete with the linking words from the text.
tasks.text: {{1}}, modding is not always simple. […] {{2}}, the relationship between companies and modders is getting better.
tasks.rationale_es: *Of course* concede un problema; *Still* (o *However*, *Even so*) vuelve a la idea positiva.
